summary: Madison Taylor's feature profiles several people who changed careers in 2023-2024, covering motivations such as layoffs, job insecurity, search for meaning, identity, and adaptability. Individuals range in age from 32 to 55 and moved into fields like culinary arts, cybersecurity, app development, social work, and sustainability. The piece argues that adaptability is the new job security and that career reinvention is not limited to the young.
one_line: Madison Taylor profiles people of varied ages who started over in new fields in 2023-2024, arguing adaptability is the new job security.
key_facts: Jacob Harrison, 35, a former marketing executive, was laid off in October 2023 and enrolled in culinary school in January 2024.
Patricia Wells, 48, an ex-real estate agent, moved into cybersecurity in March 2024 and compared re-skilling to "learning a new language at my age."
Michael Nguyen, an accountant turned app developer, changed careers after his firm downsized following a merger in December 2023.
Michael Nguyen said "adaptability is the only real security."
Sarah Johnson, 32, a mother of two and ex-pharmaceutical sales rep, pivoted to social work in September 2023 after realizing during a family vacation that her work lacked impact.
Robert Clark, 55, a former high school teacher, launched an online tutoring platform in February 2024.
Sophia Rodriguez, 40, formerly in finance, became a sustainability consultant in November 2023 to align work with her environmental activism.
Alexis Turner, 44, left the legal profession to start a non-profit in January 2024, and called it "a collective decision" involving her husband, two children, and parents.
Luke Pearson, a former automotive engineer, moved into digital marketing in April 2024 and called the choice "liberating and terrifying in equal measure."
The article says AI and automation are making many roles obsolete, so workers must pivot or be left behind.
The article contrasts the concept of a 'job for life' with a 'life of jobs.'
The article presents Robert Clark's story as defying the ageist stereotype that career reinvention is a young person's game.
